summary: This work revisits the rhombus qubit—a four-junction interferometer protected against charge noise—by intentionally introducing junction asymmetry ($\alpha = 0.63$) to raise the qubit frequency toward 100 MHz and mitigate low-frequency noise sources. The modified soft-rhombus qubit achieves $T_1 \approx 500$ μs in the biased-noise regime (away from frustration) and $T_1 \approx 27$ μs at half-flux frustration, with flux noise and quasiparticle tunneling identified as dominant loss mechanisms at low frequencies.
motivation: While the symmetric rhombus provides protection against dielectric relaxation through charge-parity symmetry, its low transition frequency exposes it to 1/$f$ flux noise and quasiparticle-induced loss, motivating investigation of how circuit modifications can shift the optimal operating regime toward higher frequencies where these noise sources are suppressed.
method: A soft-rhombus qubit was fabricated on sapphire with tantalum/aluminum-oxide junctions, where one junction has $E_J^{(4)} = 0.63 E_J$ relative to the other three. Circuit quantization, numerical simulations of multi-mode wavefunctions, and comprehensive noise analysis using Fermi's golden rule modeled relaxation from capacitive loss, drive-line coupling, flux noise ($A_\Phi = 4$ μΦ₀), and quasiparticle tunneling ($x_{qp} = 10^{-8}$).
result: Ramsey dephasing times of $T_\varphi^R \approx 90$ ns in the biased-noise regime and $\approx 670$ ns at frustration agree with flux-noise models; relaxation measurements show that introducing asymmetry reduces coupling to $\sin(\hat{\phi}_i)$ operators and shifts the performance bottleneck to several GHz, where capacitive and Purcell losses dominate over low-frequency flux and quasiparticle noise.
